content.thinking:
I'm planning the file structure for this prop group, thinking through League of Legends-style saturated glowing gem aesthetics on a floor base, and working out whether I need a root joint for the builder requirements even for static props.

I'm also figuring out the hinge mechanics for a treasure chest lid — using a "lid" joint, calculating that rotating by a negative angle about the X-axis will tip the lid open and backward correctly, and planning to build the lid geometry in its closed position before posing the joint so attached parts ride along with the rotation.

For the lid shape itself, I'm working out how to form a barrel-vault curve, either by using a half-cylinder geometry rotated into place or by extruding an arched profile with thickness along the hinge axis.

I'm sketching the arch outline points for the lid curve, keeping a small bevel of 0.015 and skipping smoothing since the shape is convex and sharp edges are fine. The lid stays a closed solid, with the interior bottom face left as bare wood visible when opened.

For the lining, I'm figuring out a thin red velvet box placed just below the lid's inner surface so it reads as visible padding from underneath rather than being hidden inside the lid geometry, settling on centering it around y=0.414 to avoid overlap.

I'm rethinking the body: instead of a solid box, I should make it a hollow open chest with floor and four walls so the gold heap is actually visible piled inside, rising above the rim as a partial dome or mound shape, with the walls sized to keep the lining fitting cleanly within the rim's inner width.

For materials, I want dark wood with a cel-shaded grain texture for the body and gold metal straps as bands, plus a lock plate on the front face with a gem-set keyhole — noting the hinge sits at the back so the lid swings open away from the front, rotating roughly 105 degrees.

I'm also adding a circular stone dais beneath the chest as a base: a lathe disc about 1.3-1.4m radius, dark purple with a gold ring and a glowing painted rune circle for that hextech-style look, sitting flush with the floor at the scene's center while the chest sits toward the back, giving an overall footprint of roughly 2.6 meters across.

Working out the chest's hinge position and rotation math, I'm placing the body center around z=-0.35 with the hinge at z=-0.63, then computing where the open lid lands after a -105° rotation about the X-axis so its top edge reaches about 0.96m up and its back edge extends to about z=-0.93, confirming the 1.3m dais radius is large enough to cover the opened lid's footprint.

Now I'm deciding the overall layout: keeping the chest centered at x=0 rather than offsetting it, placing its center at cz=-0.4, and planning its construction as walls, brass corner posts, front straps, a horizontal band, rivets, and a lock plate with a glowing gem, plus small feet at the base. I'm also establishing that the chest sits on top of the dais, so all object base heights need to start from the dais height rather than floor level.

Defining the ground reference at G=0.06, then setting the chest's width, depth, and height dimensions and its hinge position along the rim. For the coin pile spilling out front, I'm planning to generate hundreds of thin gold cylinder coins scattered with random tilt and merged by color group into a few combined meshes to keep the triangle count manageable, using varying gold tones and silver for visual variety.

I'm deciding against texturing the bulk coins since UV mapping artifacts and alpha cutouts would be messy, opting instead for a handful of individually placed "hero coins" with emblem decals leaning against the chest for visual interest. For the mound itself inside the chest, I'm sketching out a partial dome shape scaled and positioned to sit naturally within the interior.

For the gold color on the dome, I'm layering a mottled gold/darker-gold cel shading pattern rather than flat paint, then scattering coins across the surface by sampling points on the ellipsoid analytically, computing surface normals, and aligning each coin's orientation to that normal (with slight random tilt) using an "aim" helper instead of the typically-restricted quaternion method. Now I'm starting to plan a similar heap of coins spilling onto the floor in front of the chest.

Writing coin pile generation...

Still building coin geometry...

For the mound base, I'm using a scaled sphere dome with the bottom cut off, sized slightly smaller than the coin placement radius so the coins sit just above the dome surface with a small consistent gap.

For gem shapes, I'm working out profiles for faceted cuts—octahedron and icosahedron geometries for some gems, plus a custom lathe profile defining the crown and pavilion outline for a classic cut gem shape.

I'm picking a jewel-toned palette: ruby red, sapphire blue, emerald green, amethyst purple, topaz gold, and a cyan hextech accent, each gem getting its own glow effect, though I realize flat glow colors might wash out the faceted shading since emissive glow overrides per-face lighting.

I'll dial the glow strength down to around 0.4-0.45 so brightness adds without erasing the facets, then plan roughly 25 gems scattered across the piles plus a standout hero cluster of five tilted, pointed hexagonal prisms glowing cyan to act as a centerpiece crystal formation. I'm now thinking about where to place a crown on top of one of the coin piles.

Now I'm designing the crown itself as a tall, exaggerated LoL-style piece with a gold lathed band, seven curved outward-swept spikes tipped with gems, and a taller central spike, positioning it upright on its own small dedicated coin pile and calculating its base height from the pile's top surface.

For the trim rings I'll make a closed catmull ring helper and sweep a small circle around it with six sides. Then for the spikes, I'll place eight around the crown band, alternating tall and short heights, swept along bezier curves from base to tip with a tapering radius for a pointed cap.

Now I'm capping the spike tips flat with a small radius and adding a tiny gold octahedron gem on top, plus placing a larger ruby gem lathed on the front of the band oriented outward along its own axis, with several more gems spaced around.

I'm also adding a red velvet dome inside the crown rising from the band interior, shaped with a closed lathe profile, visible from above, and planning two crossing gold arcs that sweep from the band up to the crown's top.

Now I'm placing the arches along the x and z axes with curved catmull sweeps meeting at a central top point, then alternating eight spikes at 45-degree offsets between them, with a small gold orb and gem topping the center.

Next I'm planning three distinct goblets: a tall gold bejeweled one, a silver chalice, and a third ornate cup lying on its side spilling coins, built from a horizontal-axis lathe profile.

Now I'm planning the scene layout: positioning the chest, floor pile, crown pile, and the two goblets on the dais with specific coordinates, radii, and heights to arrange the composition naturally.

I'm simplifying the layout: gold goblet standing at the front right, silver goblet resting atop its coin pile, and the jeweled goblet lying tipped on its side near the front of the dais with coins spilled around it.

Working out the lathe placement for the tipped goblet, tilting its axis so the foot sits lower and the mouth lifts slightly, then scattering about 30 coins in a trail flowing out from its mouth, mostly flat with a little random tilt for realism.

Checking spacing between the front coin pile and the goblet so their footprints don't overlap, then placing the crown pile off to the side. I'm also planning extra set dressing beyond the core coins/gems/chest/crown/goblets — things like stacked coin columns, a spilled leather pouch, loose rings, a draped pearl strand, and maybe a scroll.

Adding pearl necklace and gold chain details...

Now I'm sizing the dais as a lathed disc with a flat top and a raised lip, and adding a thin gold ring trim around its outer edge for a bit of glow.

For the rune ring, I want a glowing teal rune texture on a circular plane sitting flush on the dais top, drawn as SVG concentric rings and hex-star tick marks with strokes thick enough to stay visible at render resolution, oriented facing upward so it reads correctly from the camera.

For the dais itself, I'm going with dark violet stone patches cel-shaded under normal lighting so the top surface reads as lit, and I'll add a handful of small glowing cyan crystal studs around the rim as decorative pylons.

I'm thinking 5 hex-based stone pylons spaced around the rim at radius 1.2, each with an elongated octahedron crystal glowing on top, positioned to avoid clashing with the chest lid at the back. Checking the overall scale—dais radius 1.35 puts the whole prop at about 2.7m across, which fits within the diorama size guidelines, and height stays reasonable with the lid around 1.0m and pylons plus crystals adding just a bit more.

For the chest itself, I'm adding a large glowing cyan gem atop the gold heap inside as a hero element, then building the chest body from boxed wall panels (front, back, sides, floor) with painted wood grain, a dark metal bottom trim band, and brass corner posts to frame the structure.

Still working through the strap and rib details...

Adjusting rib geometry...

For colors I'm picking a brass tone for metal fittings, and deciding to skip rivets on the lid straps but add them to the front body straps. For the hardware, I'm placing a gold lock plate on the front body wall below the rim, with a keyhole detail, plus a latch tab and hasp attached to the lid itself since it needs to open with the lid.

I'm adding a glowing ruby gem on the lock plate, small feet boxes beneath the chest body, and thinking through interior details like red velvet lining boxes visible along the inside walls when viewed from above.

Now I'm positioning the lining panels inset slightly from the inner walls with a dark crimson color, covering back, sides, and front. Then I'm working out the dome-shaped heap of treasure inside the chest, sizing it so it peaks above the rim and calculating where its ellipsoid surface intersects the chest walls.

I'm designing a gem placement helper for the pile surface - picking a surface point, orienting the gem along the outward normal with some jitter, and sinking it slightly into the pile. I'm budgeting roughly 55 gems per part across piles, dais, crown, goblets, lock and hero gem, using 8-segment lathe geometry for performance.

Now I'm mixing gem cuts: round brilliant via lathe, octahedron for a diamond-ish look, and elongated hex crystals, with small gems using fewer segments. I'm also sketching a color palette for gold, brass, and silver tones, debating whether flat colors feel too plain compared to a hand-painted style.

I'm expanding the coin palette to five or six tones for flat-shaded variety across merged coin clusters, but I need to stay mindful of total unique colors across coins, gems, chest wood, and brass elements since there's roughly a 64-color budget to work within.

For the metallic paints, I'm defining mottled cel paints for gold, brass, and silver—each using two-tone gradients with slight contrast adjustments to simulate polish and highlights on crowns, goblets, and lathe-turned parts.

I'm also sizing the paint texture atlas, estimating total painted surface area across the dais and chest to pick a texel density that keeps detail sharp without bloating resolution, settling around 1024px per sheet with coins left unpainted. For wood surfaces, I'm applying a grain-pattern cel paint with brown tones oriented along the natural axis for boxes and chests.

Now I'm positioning coin stacks on the dais, randomizing offsets so coins don't look perfectly aligned, checking each stack's distance from center stays within the dais radius, and adjusting coin thickness and radius so stacked heights look proportional and natural.

Shaping the pouch lathe profile...

That segment checks out fine too. Now I'm working out the pouch's leather coloring with a mottled cel paint and adding a red cord ring at the neck. I'm deciding to keep the pouch upright rather than tilted, positioning it near the spilled coins at its base, and checking the distance to make sure placement works geometrically.

Actually, I realize I need to restart this layout — the goblet, pile, and pouch positions keep conflicting, so I'm redefining a clean coordinate plan: chest at the back with the lid open, and the front coin pile positioned just ahead of it.

From there I'm placing a crown pile slightly to the left, checking it stays within the dais radius, then adding a silver coin pile to the right with goblet B resting on top, and a standing gold goblet A nearby.

Now I'm positioning the crystal cluster near the chest's left edge, making sure it doesn't collide with the crown pile, then laying out a pouch and three small coin stacks across the front row, and finally placing a fallen goblet C with its mouth pointing outward.

Working through where the trail of spilled coins from the goblet's mouth should land, checking it stays within the dais boundary and clear of the crystal pile's radius, then adding scattered gems near the pouch.

I'm placing the five pylons at a wider radius spaced to avoid the clutter of central objects, then wrestling with whether the pearl necklace should drape from the chest down onto the pile or simply lie resting on the dais surface — opting for the latter as simpler to place convincingly.

Working out a curved path for the necklace that follows the pile's ellipsoid surface, sweeping around in an arc with gold chain segments and merged pearl spheres strung along it, capping the design with a sapphire pendant hanging at the path's end.

I'm also thinking through bone assignment for the jewelry parts—since there's only one joint plus the lid, I need to explicitly specify which bone each piece attaches to rather than relying on nearest-joint logic, since parts near the hinge could mistakenly bind to the lid.

I'll create a helper function that wraps part creation with the bone and position arguments baked in, so I can call it concisely for every component. I'm also noting constraints for the glow effect—it needs a Part with a mesh, flat string colors rather than material names, and I should double-check how it interacts with textured surfaces.

Now I'm sketching out the SVG rune design: a layered circular glyph with concentric rings, dashed patterns, tick marks generated programmatically, and an inscribed hexagram, all centered in a 400x400 viewbox.

I want to keep the stroke colors at full opacity in bright cyan so the glyph reads clearly from a top-down view, with emissive glow applied to make the lines appear luminous. I'm also planning the dais itself to have a lathed outer ring with gold trim and a teal glow layer beneath the rune.

Setting up the dais profile and rune disc positioning to avoid z-fighting, then placing pylons radially around the dais with lathed hexagonal stone shapes and crystal tops.

Now I'm designing the crystal cluster near the pylons, using a cyan hextech palette with some violet accents, building elongated hexagonal lathe profiles for each crystal to give them a tapered faceted look.

Still placing crystal clusters...

Now I'm designing Goblet A: a gold cup with a band of six gems around its rim, a gemmed stem node, a trim ring at the rim, and a gold coin disc placed inside near the top to suggest coin contents.

Goblet B gets its own design: shorter and wider, silver-painted with a sapphire gem band, filled with a heaped gold dome of coins, positioned atop the third coin pile with its base height tied to the pile's peak. I'm now shaping its foot profile as a separate lathe path from Goblet A's.

Still checking goblet profile coordinates for overlaps...

Now I'm designing a third lying goblet C with a jeweled cup in brass and purple gem tones, scaled down from goblet A's profile, and working out the radial placement formula for its gems relative to its tilted axis.

I'm building a reusable radial-direction helper that rotates around an arbitrary axis so I can place gem bands consistently on goblet A, the crown, and this new goblet. Then I'm scattering spilled coins from goblet C's mouth across the floor, varying their distance and lateral jitter along the tilt axis and adding slight height offsets for stacking and tilt.

Now I'm working out the geometry for the lying goblet C relative to the floor — checking how the foot height and axis tilt affect where the rim touches down, since the current numbers leave the rim floating about 2cm above the floor and I need to adjust the tilt so it rests properly.

I'm also scattering loose coins across the dais and estimating overall totals: tallying up piles, heaps, stacks, trails, and spilled coins to get a rough total count (around 430), then thinking through how many triangles a 9-sided cylinder approximation for each coin would contribute.

Now I'm figuring out the gem triangle counts using lathed geometry, then designing a helper function for sampling points on a pile's dome surface, computing positions and normals parametrically so coins and gems can sit naturally on the mound shape.

For the radial distribution I want more density near the top of the pile and sparser near the edges, so I'm biasing the random sampling with a square-root curve to get area-uniform coverage in plan view.

The dome underneath gets a mottled gold paint treatment using two amber tones for a weathered coin-stack look. Then I'm thinking about adding floating four-point star sparkles above the gems and pile tops, LoL-style, using small glowing cards oriented to face the viewer along the z-axis.

For the sparkles, I'll use vertical cross-oriented cards so they're visible from the sides, generate a gold-white star shape as an SVG texture, and scatter about eight of them above the hero gem, crown tip, and gem pile positions.

For the chest lid, I'm placing a small gold disc ornament with a cyan gem center at the top of the lid arch, calculating its position from the hinge and rim coordinates so it sits centered between the ribs.

I'm checking the arch vertices to confirm the slope near the apex is gentle enough that the flat plate rests with only a tiny gap, which I compensate by sinking it slightly for a snug fit. I'm skipping the interior velvet lining and gold trim detail for now, and moving on to add four brass foot boxes at the chest's corners.

Now I'm extending those corner posts to full height as structural brass elements that protrude slightly beyond the walls, plus adding a gold base band strip along the bottom edges to avoid coplanar z-fighting with the walls. I'm also planning small rivet spheres along the corner posts at a few height levels on the front-facing side, working out their exact positions per post.

Still placing rivets and straps...

Adding plank seam detail...

For the lid I'll use plank seams based on p.z instead, spacing them every 0.09 units since the curvature there makes x-based seams awkward. Then I want to add jewelry to the hero—a large cyan diamond gem lathed near the chest—plus a palette of gem colors to reuse across pieces, with glow applied by copying the material settings. Writing gem lathe function...

Setting up coin geometry with a small cylinder shape and a palette of gold and silver tones for coin collectibles...

I'm deciding to skip fine ridge detailing on regular coins and instead add a few hero coins leaning against the pile with an emblem design—gold cylinders topped with a circular face showing a ring and star motif for visual interest.

Working out positioning so each leaning coin tilts naturally with its normal vector angled toward the viewer and slightly upward, placing the emblem decal on the front face and optionally the back for completeness.

I'm computing where each coin can sit near the pile's edge without floating off it, checking the ellipse boundary at each x-coordinate to find a valid z position that keeps the coin resting against the pile.

Now I'm designing the coin emblem as an SVG texture: a layered circle with a golden base, a lighter ring, a darker bronze ring, and a star shape in the center with highlight details for depth.

For the gem pile, I'm placing pile.gems with randomized colors from a gem palette, varying sizes, and orientations blended between the surface normal and some randomness for natural scatter.

Setting up the import scaffolding for the scene builder, including geometry merging utilities, math helpers, path curves, and texture/grain utilities before writing the actual construction code.

Now I'm defining the metadata object and starting the build function, setting up the hoard's root joint and lid hinge, with constants for the chest's width, depth, height, and rim position to control the overall proportions.

Still writing the joint setup and part helper function...

A simple box() helper builds each part from a BoxGeometry with given dimensions, color, and position, and I'm estimating part counts per object (coins, rivets, chest, gems, crown, goblets) all staying safely under 400. Now I'm defining material paints like gold and brass using mottled color blends with cel shading for texture.

For the lid seams, I'm thinking the planks follow the curve of the arch, so seams should run as rings parametrized by angle, using p.z rather than p.x, even though the lid ends might show some fine striping. Now I'm moving on to defining the dark velvet material.

I'll use a flat color with the cel shading wrapper for both red and velvet tones, since cel adds nice shading to flat colors anyway, matching the overall lighting style.

Now I'm building the dais using a lathe shape with a stone color, with a trim ring in gold near the outer edge.

Writing ring sweep code...

Now I'm adding a rune disc rendered from SVG onto a circle geometry, glowing and positioned just above the dais, checking that the texture and transparency for the thin rune lines work correctly.

I'm also generating the actual SVG markup for the rune: drawing sixty tick marks around a circle with varying lengths, small diamond glyphs at six positions, and a six-pointed star made from two overlapping triangles.

Now I'm positioning five pylons around the structure, checking their angles so they clear the chest and lid geometry, then building lathe geometry for each pylon's stone base and its glowing cyan crystal cap, using a hexagonal profile curve.

I'm moving on to constructing the chest body itself, placing wooden box panels for the front, back, and side walls while being careful about overlapping corners causing z-fighting.

Still placing interior panels...

Adding front straps with rivets, a lock plate positioned to avoid colliding with the straps, and a keyhole cutout with a small cylindrical hole beneath it.

Positioning the hasp box over the lid front with its gem accent, then placing a keyhole cutout on the plate beneath it, checking that none of these overlap the lid's arch or ribs.

I'm leaning toward a cyan hextech glow for the hasp gem paired with gold trim, while letting the other treasure gems vary in color for visual richness. Now I'm writing a helper function that maps the lid's outline points through a scale transform to generate the arch shape for extrusion.

Defining extrude parameters...

Computing rivet placement along rib positions...

Checking that the velvet lining fits within the inner opening without overlapping the walls, and confirming the lid lining sits coincident with the body rim when closed. Then I set the lid's opening pose with a rotation around the x-axis, tipping it back about 105 degrees.

Thinking through the hinge rotation direction: since the lid parts extend forward from the hinge, a positive rotation would push them down, so I need a negative angle to swing the lid up and open.

Now I'm planning the pile of coins inside the chest, defining a pile structure with center position, radii, height, and base elevation, then writing a helper function to compute coin positions distributed across an elliptical dome shape using normalized surface coordinates.

For the dome geometry itself, I'm using a partial sphere scaled to match the pile's elliptical footprint, then checking whether the open bottom of the dome would be visible—since it's floating slightly above the chest floor, but the walls should block that view from outside, so it should be fine visually.

Matching the filler color to the dome base so the top edge lines up seamlessly. Now I'm writing a helper function to scatter coins across the pile using a seeded random generator for angle, radius, and jitter so they look naturally strewn.

Adding gem scattering on top with randomized positions, axes, and colors cycling through a gem palette, plus a buckets system that groups coin geometries by color and merges each group into a single flat-shaded mesh part for efficiency.

Now I'm working out the crown geometry for pile P2, positioning its base just above the pile peak and sizing its radius relative to the pile's footprint, then starting to define the crown's band as a lathe profile.

Good, the dome sits just inside the wall, so I'll paint it as velvet. Now I'm adding trim rings in brass at specific heights and radii, plus a ring of gems alternating colors around the band.

Working out gem placement and bezel sizing...

Working out the gem placement atop each spike, checking that the pavilion cone depth seats properly against the narrow spike tip radius, then deciding to cycle gem colors across the tall spikes.

Now I'm mapping out two symmetric arches using catmull curves sweeping upward and crossing at the top, built from small gold cylindrical segments, with a gold orb and glowing cyan gem capping their intersection point.

I'm checking that the arch endpoints land within the band's metal radius without colliding with the spikes, and setting the crown jewels' glow strength to 0.45. Now I'm sketching out a reusable goblet-building function that takes a profile, material, base position, and axis vector so I can orient it vertically or along another direction for the C-shaped lying variant.

For the general goblet construction, I'm planning a `frameAxes` helper to get perpendicular vectors from any axis, placing gems and ring trims relative to the base and axis rather than assuming vertical orientation, and generalizing the circle-point generator so it works for crowns and goblets alike. I'm also laying out the goblet's rim rings, foot ring, and stem node dimensions based on the existing profile data.

I'm now thinking through how to fill each goblet's cup contents with a `filled` parameter -- gem bands and stem gems, a flat coin disc for one variant, a pile of gems for the filled cup, and a heaped dome of coins for another, each with specific colors and placements.

Adding coin palettes for the different treasure piles, mixing gold and silver tones with varied ratios per pile type.

I'm also placing a leather pouch with a tie ring, positioning a few gold coins peeking out of its open mouth.

Working out the spill coin angles and radii so they scatter toward the chest without colliding with the existing stacks, checking each proposed position against the other piles' bounds.

Then I'm sketching the coin stacks themselves—positions, rising heights, and color sequences of gold and silver—before moving to the loose gems on the dais, where I need to decide how an upright gem with a pointed pavilion should rest against the floor without sinking unnaturally.

I end up tilting the gem axis and resting it on its side instead, raising its height proportional to its radius for a believable sit. For the octahedron shapes, I'm placing them with randomized rotation and a glow effect, then checking candidate positions for the loose gems against the chest and prop regions to avoid overlap.

I settle on a handful of scattered gem coordinates near the upper right and left areas, nudging each one slightly to clear the goblet's trail, the pouch, and the crown pile boundaries.

Now I'm checking the glow strengths and placing sparkle highlights at key spots -- the hero gem, crown top, goblet rims, and pile tips -- making sure each one sits just outside the collision radius of nearby objects.

Adding a necklace path with pearls and a brass chain sweep...

I'm thinking about adding extra treasure props like a stacked pyramid of gold ingots and loose gems near the chest, working through placement coordinates so they don't overlap with the existing coins and goblets.

For the ingot shape, I'm planning to extrude a trapezoid profile with beveled edges to get a realistic tapered gold bar look, then stack a few into a small pyramid.

I need to check for overlap with the P2 crystal cluster, so I'm shifting the ingot stack's center z down to -0.2, giving rows at -0.3, -0.2, -0.1, which keeps clear of the crystal at -0.05 while staying within the chest's x boundary.

The fourth crystal at (-0.88,-0.32) overlaps the ingots, so I'm relocating it to (-1.1,-0.3), which clears the ingot x-range safely.

Now I'm working out dais pylon placements at radius 1.2, checking their angular positions against nearby objects like the goblet to avoid collisions, starting with one pylon near 200° giving coordinates around (-0.41,-1.13).

I'm checking whether this pylon clips the chest lid's rotated geometry — computing the lid's minimum z-extent after rotation gives roughly -0.99 to -1.0, so a pylon edge at -1.04 is uncomfortably close. Bumping the pylon radius to 1.25 pushes its edge to -1.085, clearing the lid, but then I notice the pylon's base profile (radius .09) now extends to 1.34, which overshoots the dais edge around 1.29–1.36, so I need to reconcile that overlap too.

Now I'm testing different placement angles for the pylons to avoid collisions with the goblets and crystals — 160° and 200° look workable, but 100° or 80° put the pylon too close to goblet A or crystal P3. Settling on symmetric back/side angles like 135° and 225° keeps enough clearance (~0.38 away from the nearest crystal), so I'm leaning toward a four-pylon layout using these angles.

Checking that goblet trail end at (-0.9,0.62) is too close to a pylon, I decide to skip the front pylon placements and simplify to just 3 back pylons, adjusting crystal cluster positions to avoid overlap near the 240° pylon location.

I settle on four pylons at 120°, 150°, 180°, and 210°, computing their coordinates and checking clearances against the crystal cluster and the lid's rear edge -- everything fits with roughly 0.6 units of spacing. Now I'm verifying the overall height budget, making sure the opened lid's maximum extent and the crystal cluster heights stay within the bounding box.

The chest's floor contact checks out at y=0 with nothing protruding below, and the lid's -105° open angle clears the rib bottoms and back wall cleanly. I also confirm the flat color palette stays under the 64-color limit once I count coins, gems, and extras, and that the brass hasp paint can be shared across parts without bloating the atlas.

Now I'm writing the gem helper that lathes an outline around an axis, with two outline shapes depending on gem kind, and wraps it in a glow effect. I need to double-check the outline winding direction since lathe normals could flip and make faces invisible if the orientation is wrong.

Checking the docs' example for a goblet-style lathe: the path must run from the axis out, up, and back, forming a counterclockwise loop. My gem outline follows the same counterclockwise pattern — axis bottom, out to girdle, up, back to axis top — so it should be consistent with the expected winding.

Checking the gem shape and lathe tip for degeneracy at the axis, then sketching out the crystal profile function parameterized by length and radius.

Hex crystals use six segments with axis tilt, and lathe smoothing defaults seem fine. I'm also typing the crystal outline arrays as OutlinePoint tuples, confirming the type accepts sharp-corner markers.

For the lid, I'm posing it on the chest's hinge bone with a backward rotation and attaching rivets merged into the lid geometry at its local origin. I set up a lidPart helper bound to the lid bone for extrusion, and the hinge rig records the joint. Finally, I'm placing the hero gem on the chest near the rim's top edge with a slight axis tilt and small radius.

Now I'm adding two more large gems scattered across the coin heap using a gemAt helper that positions them by angle and radius, plus deliberately scattering extra gems and coins onto the pile with a deterministic seeded random generator inside the build closure. Writing coin geometry setup...

Still writing coin placement logic...

Still writing ring geometry...

Still writing goblet geometry...

Adding goblet contents...

Still placing coin trail coordinates...

Now I'm writing a helper function to place parts, using proper types for colors and positions, and making sure the Fill type import matches what's used elsewhere in the codebase.

Writing crown geometry code...

Still writing spike geometry...

Adding gem/bezel proportions...

I'm skipping decals on the lid ends and banner, then moving to finalize the file -- pruning unused imports like Paint in favor of Fill, and double-checking that everything else (OutlinePoint, bezier, catmull, mergeGeometries, THREE, etc.) is actually referenced. Now I'm defining the pile data structures with typed coordinates for positioning objects on the scene.

Checking that P1's coin pile position touches the chest's front wall without clipping through the corner posts or straps, then assigning gem and coin counts per pile and starting on P3's silver-heavy color palette.

Still writing pile code...

Still placing rivets...

Attaching the lock gem and hasp gem to the lid bone too, then checking the lid's depth dimensions against the body to make sure the curve profile lines up correctly at the hinge line, adjusting the outline points so the lid depth matches the body's 0.58 depth.

With the lid geometry confirmed and hinge position verified against the body, I'm moving on to writing the glue code and the rune SVG builder.
